blocks.title: Present denominations (as per the 2024-25 syllabus)
rows: **₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500 and ₹2000** (the ₹2000 note was announced for withdrawal from circulation in May 2023 but remains legal tender).
1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 25 paise were withdrawn from **30 June 2011** and are no longer legal tender.
Printing was **discontinued** because these denominations are now coins.

blocks.text: The currency of India is the **Indian Rupee (INR)** and one rupee has **100 paise**. The rupee symbol ₹ combines the Devanagari letter 'Ra' and the Latin capital 'R', with a **double horizontal line** at the top. Notes are called **banknotes** because they are issued by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**.

blocks.title: Mahatma Gandhi Series
blocks.text: By **Notification no. 2652 dated 8 November 2016**, the Government withdrew the legal tender status of **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series issued till that date. All currency notes carry the Governor's signature except the **₹1 note**, which is issued by the Government and signed by the Finance Secretary.

blocks.title: Coins and notes in a line
blocks.phrase: Coins: 1-2-5-10 ('One Two Five Ten'). Notes: 10-20-50-100-200-500-2000 – every note starts at ten, ₹2 and ₹5 became coins.
letters: Paise coins up to 25 paise lose legal tender

sections.title: Who does what: RBI and Government

blocks.title: RBI versus Government of India
rows: Central Government, on recommendation of the RBI Central Board
Government, on the advice of the RBI
Coinage, design and minting of coins

blocks.title: What the RBI does in currency management
items: Derives its currency role from the **RBI Act, 1934**.
Coordinates with the Government on **banknote design and security features**.
Estimates denomination-wise requirement and places an **indent** with printing presses.
Aims to give the public **good quality notes**: notes returned from circulation are examined, fit ones are reissued, soiled and mutilated ones are destroyed.
Acts as the agent of the Government of India for distribution and administration of currency.

blocks.title: Notes = RBI, Coins = Government
blocks.phrase: 'N-R, C-G': Notes by RBI (Section 25 and 26 of the 1934 Act), Coins by Government (Coinage Act 2011).
letters: Notes: RBI Act 1934; design approved by Centre under Section 25
Coins: Government of India, Coinage Act 2011
Liability to pay on demand; the promise clause

blocks.title: Who decides the design
blocks.text: The RBI does not alone decide the design of a note. The **Central Government** approves it on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board, in consultation with the RBI.

sections.title: Limits, languages and the promise clause

blocks.title: Rules under the Acts
rows: The RBI Act allows notes of ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 or any other denomination the Centre specifies, but **never above ₹10,000**.
Coins can be issued up to **₹1,000** under the Coinage Act, 2011.
**Hindi** at the centre, **English** on the reverse and **fifteen other languages** in the language panel.
'I promise to pay the bearer the sum of rupees …' under **Section 26**; the RBI's liability arises from **statute**, not contract.

blocks.text: The promissory clause means the banknote is a **legal tender for the stated amount**. The RBI's obligation is to **exchange** the note for notes of lower value or for coins that are legal tender under the Coinage Act, 2011, of equal value.

blocks.title: 10:1 rule for the highest value
blocks.phrase: Notes up to ₹10,000, coins up to ₹1,000 – one-tenth for coins.
letters: 15 panel languages plus Hindi and English

blocks.title: High-value notes of the past
blocks.text: The highest denomination ever printed by the RBI was the **₹10,000 note**, first in **1938** and again in **1954**. High-value notes were demonetised in **1946** and again in **1978**.

blocks.title: Issue offices and chests
items: The RBI manages currency operations through its **Issue Offices** at Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Belapur, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Guwahati, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Jammu, Kanpur, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai, Nagpur, New Delhi, Patna and Thiruvananthapuram, plus a currency chest at Kochi.
**Mint-linked offices** at **Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai and New Delhi** first receive coins from the mints and pass them to other RBI offices.
Banknotes and rupee coins are stocked at **currency chests**; small coins at **small coin depots**.
The RBI has over **4,075 currency chests**, and around **3,746 bank branches** act as small coin depots (as per the 2024-25 book).

blocks.title: Movement of currency
items: Chests distribute currency to branches depending on **specific demand**; branches demand based on **business volume**.
Specially built **trucks** serve short distances (journey finished within the day) and **railways** serve long distances, guarded by police; remittances to chests are accompanied by RBI officials.
Movement from a chest to a branch is the **responsibility of the bank** concerned.
Banks replenish ATMs based on **daily withdrawal propensity**; many outsource off-site ATM replenishment.

blocks.title: The mint-linked four
blocks.phrase: 'HKMD' – Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, Delhi receive coins first from the mints.

sections.title: When notes and coins come back

blocks.title: Life of a returned banknote
items: Unfit notes are destroyed by shredding

blocks.text: Notes that are **fit for reissue** go back into circulation, while the **unfit** ones are **destroyed by shredding** after examination. **Coins do not come back** from circulation, except those that are withdrawn.

blocks.title: Where processing happens
blocks.text: Returned banknotes are deposited at **RBI Issue Offices**, where they are authenticated and sorted into fit and unfit lots.

blocks.title: Types of damaged notes
rows: Dirty and slightly cut; notes of ₹10 and above in **two pieces** (numbers on both ends) also count
Any public sector bank branch, currency chest branch of a private bank or RBI Issue Office; **no form** needed
A **missing portion** or composed of **more than two pieces**; refund as per RBI (Note Refund) Rules
Same places as soiled notes, **without filling any form**
Wholly or partly **obliterated, shrunk, washed, altered or indecipherable** (but not a mutilated note)
Badly damaged, fragile or burnt notes
**Only at an RBI Issue Office**, Claims Section of the Issue Department

blocks.title: Essential portions of a note
items: **Ashoka Pillar emblem** or **portrait of Mahatma Gandhi**

blocks.title: TLR facility
rows: **Triple Lock Receptacle**: the public takes a TLR cover from the RBI Enquiry Counter, fills in name, address and denominations, closes it and drops it in the receptacle against a **paper token**.

blocks.title: S-M-I: three kinds of damaged note
blocks.phrase: Soiled = Slightly cut and Stained; Mutilated = Missing or More than two pieces; Imperfect = Illegible, washed or altered.
letters: Dirty, slightly cut, or two pieces with both numbers
Missing portion or more than two pieces

blocks.title: Number of pieces
blocks.text: **Two pieces** (with numbers on both ends) = **soiled**. **More than two pieces** or a missing part = **mutilated**.

blocks.title: Where Indian currency is produced
rows: Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India (SPMCIL)

blocks.title: Four presses, four mints
blocks.phrase: Presses: 'Nashik-Dewas for SPMCIL, Mysuru-Salboni for RBI'. Mints: 'My Home Kolkata Noida' = Mumbai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Noida.

blocks.title: Karnataka and Bengal
blocks.text: RBI's own note presses are in **Mysuru (Karnataka)** and **Salboni (West Bengal)**; the SPMCIL presses are in **Nashik** and **Dewas**.

The RBI continuously works to provide **good quality banknotes** to the public. The **Clean Note Policy** contains initiatives and instructions to keep currency notes clean, and the public is asked to help the RBI and the banking system.

blocks.title: What the public should do
items: **Do not write on or rubber-stamp** banknotes or put any other mark on them.

blocks.title: Three don'ts
blocks.text: No stapling, no stamping or writing, no careless storage: this is the Clean Note Policy in one line.

blocks.title: Objectives
rows: Stop the **funding of militancy and terrorism** from across the border; counterfeit notes had been found in large numbers in terror-affected states.

blocks.title: Likely implications (mixed results)
items: Builds the confidence of the international community that India is serious about fighting corruption, helping its **ease of doing business** and corruption rankings.
Short-term **cash shortage** could reduce agricultural output, as it came near the sowing season, and spill over into industry and services.
Consumption and business investment, which depend more on overall climate and interest rates, may not be affected by a short liquidity squeeze.
People may fear depositing money in banks and may shift to **gold and real estate**.
Cash-based sectors such as transport, local markets and rural shops are hit; low business volumes in rural areas make card-reading equipment costly to install.

blocks.title: Demonetisation episodes
items: High-value notes of ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 demonetised again.
₹500 and ₹1,000 notes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series lose legal tender status.

blocks.title: Demonetisation dates
blocks.phrase: '46, '78, '16 – every time with a big note: Britain-era 1946, Janata-era 1978, and 8 November 2016.

blocks.title: Milestones of Indian currency
items: Paper currency introduced by the British government (Paper Currency Act).
RBI Act passed; it later governs RBI’s role in issuing banknotes.
**Decimal coinage** introduced (Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955); rupee = 100 paise.
Coins up to 25 paise withdrawn from circulation.

blocks.title: Odd facts that get asked
items: The ₹2000 note carries an image of **Mangalyaan** (Mars Orbiter Mission) on the reverse.
The **Kuwaiti Dinar (KWD)** is the highest-valued currency against the Indian rupee, widely called the world's strongest currency (about ₹267 per dinar at the time of writing).
The Banking Companies Act was amended in 1949 and renamed the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

blocks.title: Years to fix in memory
blocks.phrase: Paper 1861, Big note 1938, Decimal 1957: 'Paper Bags Dance' = 61, 38, 57.

blocks.title: 1955 versus 1957
blocks.text: The decimal coinage **Act** is of **1955**, but decimal coins began on **1 April 1957**. Questions can ask for either year.

revision: Coins now issued: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10; paise coins up to 25 paise withdrawn from 30 June 2011.
Banknotes: ₹10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 2000; ₹2 and ₹5 notes are no longer printed because they became coins.
RBI's role comes from the RBI Act, 1934; Section 25 needs Centre's approval of note design; Section 26 gives the promise clause.
Coinage and minting are Government of India's responsibility under the Coinage Act, 2011.
Notes cannot be above ₹10,000 under the RBI Act; coins can be issued up to ₹1,000.
Language panel shows fifteen languages, with Hindi at the centre and English on the reverse.
Currency flow: printing presses → RBI offices → currency chests → bank branches → public.
Mint-linked RBI offices: Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai and New Delhi.
Soiled: dirty or slightly cut; mutilated: missing portion or more than two pieces; exchange without any form.
Excessively soiled, brittle or burnt notes are exchanged only at RBI Issue Offices; TLR covers help for mutilated notes.
Note presses: Nashik, Dewas (SPMCIL) and Mysuru, Salboni (RBI); mints: Mumbai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Noida.
Clean Note Policy: do not staple, write on or stamp notes.
Highest note ever printed: ₹10,000 in 1938 and 1954; high-value notes demonetised in 1946 and 1978.
Decimal coinage began on 1 April 1957; paper currency began in 1861; 8 November 2016 demonetised ₹500 and ₹1,000.
